title: Why a PR should have one purpose
question: A junior's first PR adds a CSV export button, fixes an unrelated typo bug on the login page and upgrades a small library. A teammate asks to split it into separate PRs. What is the main reason?
options: Reviewers are only allowed to approve changes that touch a single folder, so mixed PRs cannot be approved at all
Each PR can be reviewed with full attention, tested on its own and reverted without undoing unrelated work
Small PRs are merged by CI faster because the pipeline skips tests for any change under a fixed number of lines
A PR that mixes several changes is rejected by Git itself unless every commit in it has the same author and date
explanation: A PR with one purpose gives the reviewer a single question to answer, makes failures easier to trace to one change, and lets the team revert it cleanly if it breaks something. Nothing in Git or most CI setups blocks mixed PRs or skips tests by size, and review rules about folders are about ownership, not about purpose.

title: What a good PR description contains
question: You finished a bug fix and are about to open the PR. Which description helps reviewers the most?
options: A one-line summary such as 'Fixes the bug', since the diff already shows exactly what changed in every file
A complete list of every file touched with the number of added and removed lines, copied from the PR page
What changed and why, how you tested it or how to try it, and a link to the issue
A short apology for the size of the change plus a request to approve quickly because a deadline is near
explanation: The diff shows what lines changed, not the reason, the intended behaviour or how to verify it. A description that states the why, the testing steps (screenshots help for UI) and the linked issue lets reviewers judge the change without guessing. File lists duplicate the PR page, and pressure to approve fast does not help anyone review well.

title: Reviewing your own diff first
question: Your code works and the tests pass locally. What is the best step before you request a review from a teammate?
options: Request the review immediately, because finding problems is the reviewer's job and reading it twice wastes time
Rewrite the whole change once more from scratch so the final version has no trace of your earlier attempts
Read your own diff on the PR page as if you were the reviewer and remove leftovers like debug logs
Ask a second teammate to read the code aloud with you before anyone else is allowed to see the pull request
explanation: A self-review catches stray `console.log` calls, commented-out code, unrelated edits and missing tests, which saves reviewers' time and shows care. Reading the diff in the PR view changes how you see it. Handing off unchecked work wastes the reviewer's attention, a full rewrite is out of proportion, and a read-aloud session is unnecessary overhead for a normal change.

title: When to open a draft PR
question: You are halfway through a feature and want feedback on the overall approach before polishing it. Tests are not written yet. What should you do?
options: Open a normal PR with 'please ignore the failing checks' in the title so reviewers know it is unfinished
Keep the branch private until every test and edge case is done, because early code only confuses reviewers
Merge the half-finished work into the main branch behind a comment so teammates can see it in the code
Open a draft pull request and say which part you want feedback on, then mark it ready later
explanation: A draft PR signals that the work is not ready for a full review, avoids notifying code owners for approval too early, and still lets teammates comment on direction when a wrong approach is cheapest to fix. Normal PRs with warnings in the title invite confusion, waiting until the end delays feedback, and merging unfinished code to main puts everyone's work at risk.

title: A red CI check on your PR
question: You opened a PR and a required CI check fails with a lint error in a file you edited. No reviewer has looked at it yet. What is the best next move?
options: Leave it as is and mention in a comment that lint rules are only about style, so reviewers can ignore the red check
Disable that lint rule in the shared configuration so the check passes without touching your own code
Close the PR and open a new one with the same code, hoping the checks run again and turn green by themselves
Fix the lint error, push the fix and make sure the checks pass before asking anyone to review
explanation: Reviewers expect checks to be green so they can spend time on design and correctness instead of things a tool already catches. Fixing the failure in your own change is quick and respectful of their time. Weakening a shared rule affects everyone and needs its own discussion, and reopening the PR hides the problem rather than fixing it.

title: Formatter noise buried in a PR
question: You changed 10 lines in a service file. Your editor reformatted the whole file on save, so the diff now shows 400 changed lines. What is the best way to handle it before requesting review?
options: Keep everything and add a comment saying the real change is somewhere inside the diff, since reviewers can use search
Ask reviewers to enable the 'hide whitespace changes' option and approve, because that makes the diff small enough
Revert the formatting-only edits so the diff shows just your change, and send any wider reformat as its own PR
Squash the formatting into your earlier commits so the history looks tidy and nobody can tell it was a separate step
explanation: Reformatting noise hides the real change, so a reviewer may miss a bug among hundreds of cosmetic lines and `git blame` gets polluted. Restoring the untouched lines, or moving a team-wide reformat to a separate PR (ideally enforced by a shared formatter config), keeps the review focused. Whitespace toggles do not hide reordered code, and squashing only hides the noise in the history.

title: Merging a big feature in small pieces
question: Your feature will take two weeks and touches the API, the UI and a migration. Teammates want small PRs, but a half-built screen must not appear for real users. What approach fits best?
options: Keep one long-lived branch and open a single PR at the end, so main never contains unfinished work
Merge the pieces as they are and tell users in the release notes that some screens are still being built
Split the work into small PRs but hold them all and merge them in one batch the night before the release
Merge small PRs one by one with the unfinished entry point hidden behind a feature flag, then turn it on at the end
explanation: A feature flag (or simply an unreachable route) lets incomplete code ship safely, so each PR stays small, reviewed and integrated early, which avoids painful conflicts. A single huge PR at the end is hard to review and risky, showing unfinished screens harms users, and holding small PRs until the last night keeps every drawback of a big one.

title: Commit messages that help reviewers
question: Your PR has commits named 'wip', 'fix', 'fix again' and 'asdf'. The team merges with a merge commit, so these messages stay in the history. What is the best improvement?
options: Leave them, because the PR title and description are the only place where anyone ever reads about the change
Rewrite them, before review starts, into messages with a short subject saying what changed and a body explaining why
Add a final commit named 'cleanup' that lists all the earlier messages so the history is explained in one place
Delete the branch and recommit everything as a single commit named 'update' so the history has no noise
explanation: Commit messages are read months later during `git log`, `git blame` and bisects, so a clear subject and a 'why' body are valuable when the history is kept. Rewriting local history is fine before others have reviewed or built on it. A trailing 'cleanup' commit adds noise, one giant 'update' commit loses the logical steps, and PR text alone does not travel with the commits.

title: What 'nit:' means in a comment
question: A reviewer comments on your PR: 'nit: `cnt` could be `count`'. How should you read this comment?
options: As a demand that blocks the merge until you rename every variable in the file to follow the same style
As a warning that the reviewer believes the code has a bug and plans to reject the PR if it is not fixed
As a minor, optional polish suggestion that should not block the merge; apply it if you agree
As a sign that the reviewer is unhappy with you personally and wants a different person to finish the task
explanation: By common convention, 'nit' (nitpick) marks a small preference, such as naming or style, that the author can take or leave without holding up the merge. Blocking issues are usually stated plainly or marked as required. Reading a nit as a bug report or as a personal judgment adds stress the comment never intended.

title: A vague review comment
question: A reviewer leaves a comment on your function: 'This feels fragile.' You do not see what they mean. What is the best reply?
options: Reply 'Done' and change something small nearby, so the thread can be closed without a long conversation
Resolve the thread without a reply, since a comment that vague cannot be required to be acted on
Escalate to the team lead right away, because unclear feedback is a sign the review process is not working
Ask which situation worries them, for example 'Do you mean an empty list or a timeout? I can add a test for it'
explanation: Feedback is only useful if you understand it, and a specific, friendly question turns a vague worry into something you can fix or test, often teaching you a failure mode. Pretending to address it leaves the real concern in the code, silently resolving the thread ignores the reviewer, and escalating a single unclear comment skips the easiest step: asking.

title: The same comment on three PRs
question: On your last three PRs, reviewers asked you for tests of the error path each time. Your fourth PR is almost ready. What is the most effective response to this pattern?
options: Wait for the reviewer to point it out again, since their comments are the official checklist for the team
Add 'error paths tested?' to your self-review checklist and apply it to the fourth PR before requesting review
Write tests for error paths only in the PRs where the reviewer has been known to ask for them
Ask the team to stop requesting error-path tests because they slow down the PRs of newer developers
explanation: Repeated comments are a free map of your blind spots. Turning them into a self-review habit means the issue is gone before review, which saves everyone a round trip and builds trust quickly. Waiting to be told again keeps the cost on the reviewer, testing only for certain reviewers misses the point of the practice, and asking to drop a team standard avoids the learning.

title: Pushing fixes during an open review
question: A reviewer left six comments on your PR. You fixed them locally. How should you push the changes while the review is still in progress?
options: Push the fixes as new commits and reply on each thread, so the reviewer can see exactly what changed since their review
Squash everything into one commit and force-push, so the PR looks as if it had been right from the start, so the history shows one tidy commit and no sign of the earlier review rounds
Close the PR and open a new one with the fixed code, so the old comments do not distract anyone
Edit the code directly in the base branch and tell the reviewer to compare it with the earlier version
explanation: New commits let the reviewer look at only the delta, which makes the second round quick; you can squash at merge time if the team prefers a clean history. Force-pushing during review rewrites the commits and can make 'changes since last review' unreliable and hide what moved. A new PR loses the discussion, and editing the base branch directly bypasses review.

title: Closing out review threads
question: You addressed most comments, but you chose not to follow one suggestion because it would change the public API. What is the best way to respond to that thread?
options: Reply explaining your reasoning in a sentence or two and offer to follow up separately if the reviewer still prefers it
Leave the thread unanswered and push the other fixes, since silence will be read as a reasonable decision
Mark the thread as resolved without a reply, because the reviewer can always reopen it if they disagree
Reply 'Will do' now and quietly skip the change, so the review can move forward without a debate
explanation: Every comment deserves an answer: what you did or why you did not. A short reason lets the reviewer decide whether the concern still stands and keeps trust high, whereas silence or a silent resolve looks like you missed the comment. Promising a change you will not make is misleading and tends to surface later at a worse time.

title: Comments waiting for days
question: You got review comments on Monday morning, but urgent work took over. It is now Wednesday and the PR is still waiting on you. What is the best move?
options: Tell the reviewer now that you are on it with a rough date, then address the comments in one batch
Wait until the work is perfect and then answer all comments at once, since a late but flawless reply is better
Ask the reviewer to take over the changes, since they already know exactly what they want from the code
Push a quick fix for only the easiest comment and mark the whole PR as ready again without saying anything
explanation: A stalled PR blocks the reviewer's context and often causes conflicts with main, so a short heads-up with an expected date keeps them informed and trusting you. Batching the fixes into one update is respectful of their time. Going silent until it is perfect leaves them guessing, handing over your PR is not their job, and a partial fix with no note looks like you skipped the rest.

title: Two reviewers ask for opposite changes
question: One reviewer asks you to extract a 40-line block into a helper. Another reviewer, on the same PR, asks you to inline the helper you already have because indirection hurts readability. What is the best way to proceed?
options: Apply whichever comment arrived first and resolve the other thread, because timing is a fair tie-breaker, on the theory that the order in which the comments were posted shows which concern the team cares about more
Reply in one thread tagging both, summarise the trade-off, and ask them to agree, or check the team style guide or ask the tech lead
Apply the request of the more senior reviewer and ignore the other, since seniority decides technical questions
Implement a third structure that partly satisfies both comments, without telling them, to avoid any conflict
explanation: When feedback conflicts, the author should not be the arbiter or silently pick a side. Making the conflict visible, with a neutral summary, lets the two reviewers or the style guide decide, and escalating to a lead is reasonable if they cannot. First-come or seniority rules ignore the technical reasons, and a hidden compromise may satisfy nobody and surprises both reviewers.

title: A suggestion that would add a bug
question: A senior teammate asks you to simplify your date handling by dropping the explicit UTC conversion. You believe it will shift report dates for users in other time zones. What is the best response?
options: Make the change as requested, because a senior has more experience and any bug can be fixed after the merge, and plan to fix any date problem later if users report it after release
Keep your version and resolve the thread, because you know this code better than someone who only skimmed it
Reply that the suggestion is wrong and cite years of programming experience from articles you once read
Share a small failing test or example showing the wrong date, explain it politely, and ask whether you are missing context
explanation: Evidence turns a disagreement about opinions into something both people can inspect, and framing it as a question leaves room for context you may lack. Following a request you believe is harmful ships a known bug, overriding a reviewer without discussion damages trust, and arguing from authority, yours or theirs, convinces nobody. If the evidence still does not settle it, accept the team's decision.

title: Reviewing when you are the newest
question: You joined a month ago and are added as a reviewer on a teammate's PR. You think you are too new to say anything useful. What is the best view?
options: Approve quickly without reading, since only people who have been on the team for years can find real problems
Decline the review and say you will start reviewing after your first year, so you do not slow the team down
Only comment on topics you are fully certain about and skip everything that you would have to ask about
Review anyway: fresh eyes spot unclear names, missing tests and confusing code, and your questions help the author
explanation: Reviewers do not need to know everything: if you cannot understand the code, others will struggle too, so your confusion is useful signal. You can also check tests, naming and edge cases. Rubber-stamping defeats the purpose, opting out of reviews slows your own learning, and staying silent when unsure removes the questions that are most valuable.

title: Phrasing a question about confusing code
question: You do not understand why a teammate's code retries a payment call three times. Which review comment is the best?
options: 'This retry logic makes no sense and looks wrong. Please rewrite it the way the rest of the codebase does it.', because consistency with the existing code matters more than the author's reasons for this version
'I'm not sure I follow why we retry three times here. Is the gateway flaky? A short comment could help future readers.'
'Why?' left on the line, since a short question avoids sounding critical and leaves the author to explain.
'Is this the right approach? It seems off to me, but I cannot say why. I will leave it to your judgement.'
explanation: A good question names what is unclear, assumes there may be a reason, and suggests a concrete outcome such as a comment or test. The harsh comment assumes the author is wrong and demands a rewrite without evidence, a bare 'Why?' is too terse to act on, and a vague 'seems off' makes the author guess what you want without giving anything to answer.

title: Checking a change beyond the diff
question: A PR changes form validation. The diff reads fine, but you are not sure what happens with an empty field or a very long name. What is the most valuable thing to do?
options: Approve based on the diff alone, because the author already ran the code and repeating it is duplicated work
Write a long comment guessing how the form might fail, without trying it, so the author can look into it later
Check out the branch, run the tests and the app, and try those inputs yourself, then report what you saw
Ask the author to record a video of every possible input before you agree to look at the change again
explanation: Reading a diff cannot show behaviour. Running the branch lets a newer person contribute real evidence, such as an unhandled empty value, instead of speculation, and it also teaches how the feature works. Approving without checking trusts luck, an unverified list of guesses wastes the author's time, and asking for videos shifts your own job onto them.

title: Preference or a real problem
question: While reviewing, you notice a variable you would have named differently and a function that can throw on a null input. How should you handle these two points?
options: Block the PR on the naming and the null case equally, so the author sees that both matter to you
Flag the null case as a real concern, and either skip the naming or label it as an optional 'nit'
Skip both comments, because a newcomer's remarks can annoy people and the code probably works anyway
Mention the naming only, since it is quick to explain and avoids a long discussion about the null case
explanation: Reviewers should focus on correctness, tests and clarity, and keep personal taste out of the way or clearly optional. A possible null error affects users, so it deserves a clear comment; a taste-based rename should not hold the merge. Treating them as equal blocks the PR on trivia, staying silent hides a real defect, and commenting on naming alone swaps the important point for the easy one.

title: Approving what you understood
question: You reviewed a PR and understood the UI part well, but the database migration was beyond you. A senior is also on the review. What is the most honest way to approve?
options: Approve or comment on the parts you covered and say clearly that you did not review the migration
Approve with 'LGTM' and nothing else, since the senior will catch anything you missed in the migration
Refuse to leave any review, since a partial review is worse for the author than no review at all
Request changes on the migration just to be safe, since you cannot confirm that it is correct yourself
explanation: An approval tells others what has been checked, so stating the scope you covered keeps it honest and tells the senior where to look. A bare LGTM suggests full coverage and can create false confidence, skipping the review loses your useful input on the UI, and requesting changes without a concrete problem blocks the author with no information to act on.

title: A review that is taking all afternoon
question: A teammate's 700-line PR has taken you two hours and you are only halfway through, while your own tasks wait. What is the best way to handle the rest of the review?
options: Say which parts you covered, ask the author to split the change or walk you through it, and agree on a time for the rest
Skim the rest very quickly and approve, so the author is not left waiting and your own tasks can resume, since the PR has to be merged today and a delayed review would look bad for the whole team
Keep reviewing until you finish line by line, even if that takes the rest of the day and delays your own work
Close the PR tab and wait for someone else to review it, hoping the author does not notice your silence
explanation: Review time is limited, and a PR too large to review well is a signal to the author. Reporting what you covered, suggesting a split or a short walkthrough and setting an expectation for the remainder keeps the review useful. A rushed approval pretends to a quality you did not apply, an endless session starves your own work, and quietly leaving makes the author wait without knowing why.

title: Spotting a possible issue in a senior's PR
question: A very senior teammate's PR queries the database inside a loop over orders. You suspect it will run hundreds of queries, but you feel nervous about commenting. What is the best action?
options: Comment on that line with your reasoning as a question, such as 'Could this run one query per order? I may be missing context.'

Say nothing, since a senior has surely considered performance and a junior's remark would be out of place, on the assumption that someone at that level would not welcome a question from a newer teammate
Approve and send a private message to the manager listing the problems you found in the senior's code
Rewrite the loop yourself in a new commit on their branch so the issue is fixed without any discussion
explanation: The goal of review is better code, not hierarchy, and seniors usually welcome a precise, respectful question; even if you are wrong, you learn something. Silence leaves a likely performance bug in place, going to a manager behind the author's back skips the direct conversation and erodes trust, and pushing commits to someone else's branch overrides their ownership without agreement.

title: A credential inside a PR
question: A teammate's PR adds an `application-test.yml` containing what looks like a real cloud API key, with the note 'only for tests'. What is the best review response?
options: Approve it, because test configuration files are never used in production so a key there cannot cause any harm, because the file only lives in the test folder and the key is probably restricted to a sandbox
Ask the author to rename the file so that scanners ignore it, and approve once the key is no longer visible
Flag it as a blocking concern, ask for the key to be removed from the PR and rotated, and suggest using a secret store or a fake value
Leave a non-blocking comment suggesting a secret manager for later and approve so the delivery date is kept
explanation: A real key committed to the repository is exposed to everyone with access, and Git history keeps it even after the file is deleted, so it must be revoked or rotated and replaced by a secret store or a fake value. Test files are often copied or shipped, hiding the file from scanners only hides the risk, and treating a leaked credential as a later improvement leaves it live.
